newsitem.title: RWANDA: UNHCR chief appeals to Rwandan refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR chief appeals to Rwandan refugees in Zaire.

text.p: The head of the U.N. refugee agency on Friday tried a radio message to lure home to Rwanda hundreds of thousands of refugees in eastern Zaire, where fighting has put them on the move again.

U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata's message was broadcast on Rwandan state radio and on a U.N.-backed radio station that transmits to camps in Zaire holding 1.1 million Rwandan refugees.

Nearly 300,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees have been forced out of camps in South Kivu province into other camps or the hills by fighting between Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels and the Zairean army.
Aid workers say refugees have received no international aid since arriving in camps near the town of Bukavu because field workers are not allowed to reach them because of security concerns.
"I am deeply saddened that once again you are on the roads fleeing for your lives," said Ogata, who is Japanese.

"I am afraid this terrible situation may not stop immediately, and I would like you to know that we will do everything possible, in cooperation with the authorities to help you where we can," she added.
"Because of your current ordeal, I am sure you will consider where you will be safer -- in Rwanda or Zaire. That is a decision for you to make.

"However, I am sincerely asking you to remember that 80,000 refugees have recently returned to Rwanda from Burundi, and UNHCR and U.N. human rights observers report that they are now resuming busy lives," she said.
Rwanda and Burundi, which both have Tutsi-dominated armies and are accused by Zaire of helping the Banyamulenge, have denied any link with the fighting. Rwanda has urged its refugees to return.

Similar appeals by UNHCR and Rwanda have largely fallen on deaf ears since the 1.1 million Hutus fled to Zaire from their homeland in 1994 in fear of reprisals for the Hutu genocide of up to an estimated one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Another 200,000 Hutus have fled from Burundi to escape war and massacres between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels.
Fighting between Zairean troops and the Banyamulenge flared a week ago around the Zairean town of Uvira near the border with Burundi. More than 200,000 Hutu refugees in camps in the area took flight.
The Banyamulenge, who migrated from Rwanda late in the 18th century, accuse Zaireans of trying to force them to leave.
A Banyamulenge spokesman in Rwanda said on Thursday they had joined forces with Zairean groups of Kaasai, Shaba and Katangese and captured three eastern towns -- Kamanyola, Nyangezi and Bwegera.
The Kaasai, Shaba and Katangese have led armed opposition to President Mobutu Sese Seko off and on since the 1960s.
The spokesman said the 300,000 Banyamulenge wanted the return of property stolen by troops and militiamen and the granting of Zairean citizenship, denied to them in 1981.
Aid groups have expressed fears about lack of food for the flood of refugees descending on Bukavu and its outskirts, saying they could also face epidemics unless they receive assistance.
Refugees arriving in their thousands are directed towards a camp at Nyamarengwe, about 20 km (12 miles) to the southwest. Many had harrowing tales of their five days on the move.
"There were women giving birth on the road. There were old men and women collapsing with exhaustion," Georges Nzohikera, a Hutu from Burundi, said.
